## Why the same order can take different amounts of time

Distance and item count alone cannot describe every delivery. Waiting, staffing, traffic and unobserved processing stages introduce uncertainty. Rather than claiming each input has one deterministic fulfilment time, we can model a conditional distribution.

$$
p(t\mid d,n,\theta).
$$

The symbol means a distribution of possible times $t$ conditional on distance $d$, item count $n$ and model parameters $\theta$. The distribution is **not** a statement that all deliveries follow a Gaussian law.

## Events and Bayes' rule

In our invented six-order dataset, three recorded times are at least 16 minutes. If a row is selected uniformly at random, the empirical event probability is $3/6=0.5$.

If $L$ denotes 'late' and $D$ denotes 'distance at least 4 km', Bayes' rule states

$$
P(L\mid D)=\frac{P(D\mid L)P(L)}{P(D)},\qquad P(D)>0.
$$

In this particular artificial dataset, all long-distance observations are late. It would be a serious mistake to infer that a new long-distance order is **certain** to be late. The sample is tiny and purposely constructed.

## From a likelihood to a posterior

A Gaussian noise model might assume

$$
T\mid\mu,\sigma^2\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2),
\qquad
p(\theta\mid\mathcal D)\propto p(\mathcal D\mid\theta)p(\theta).
$$

Likelihood quantifies consistency with observations; a prior represents information assumed before seeing the data; the posterior updates those assumptions.

Learn these concepts in [Probability and Distributions](chapters/06-probability-and-distributions/index.qmd), then use them in [Bayesian Linear Regression](chapters/09-linear-regression/bayesian-linear-regression.qmd) and [Gaussian Mixture Models](chapters/11-gaussian-mixture-models/index.qmd).

~~~bash
python3 ai-mathematics/examples/delivery_ml_lab.py probability
~~~

A mathematical probability is meaningful only after its sample space, event definition and model assumptions are made explicit.
